theBigPicture: The seven-month Iran war took another alarming turn with a missile reportedly fired at an international airport just as passengers were landing, while a new Saudi-led defense pact is pulling Pakistani and Turkish troops into the fight against the Houthis. At home and abroad, wallets are feeling it: US mortgage rates just hit a three-year high and oil remains near $125 a barrel because of the conflict. Meanwhile, France's student protests have ballooned to nearly 460 schools, forcing the government to suspend stun grenades after a teenager lost his hand.

householdImpact.energyAndFuel: Oil is trading near $125 a barrel because of the war, which keeps gas pump prices painfully high for drivers. The President is floating a pause on the federal gas tax to offer some relief, but as long as the conflict continues, expect prices at the pump to stay elevated.
householdImpact.borrowingAndMortgages: US mortgage rates have hit their highest level in three years, and loan applications have sunk to their lowest point since February, making this a tough moment to buy or refinance a home. Car loans and credit card rates tend to move in the same direction, so borrowing costs across the board remain painful.
householdImpact.groceriesAndSupplyChain: With oil this expensive, it costs more to ship, truck, and fly food around the world, and those costs eventually land on grocery shelves. Expect a slow creep in prices on imported goods and anything that travels far to reach your cart.
householdImpact.jobsAndSavings: Stock markets are surprisingly calm right now, which is good news for 401(k) balances, but the calm masks real strain in rate-sensitive corners of the economy. Housing and construction jobs are most exposed if high mortgage rates keep buyers away.

globalFlashpoints.summary: Kyiv is facing disruptions to water and power supplies with electric transit suspended, and emergency rolling blackouts have been introduced across several Ukrainian regions.

A missile was reportedly fired at an international airport just before passengers landed, Pakistan has confirmed troop deployments to Saudi Arabia under a new defense pact, and Houthi attacks in Yemen killed six this week.
Public anger is growing in Japan after a US Marine was arrested over the killing of a woman, straining local sentiment but not escalating into broader instability.

France's student protests have spread to nearly 460 schools and prompted the government to suspend stun grenades after a 15-year-old lost his hand, while large-scale protests over voting rules continue in India.

topStories.headline: France Suspends Stun Grenades After Teen Loses Hand in Student Protests
topStories.whyItMatters: With nearly 460 schools now affected and a 15-year-old seriously injured, France's government is under pressure to negotiate with students demanding fixes to understaffing and a university admissions system they call a lottery. The unrest is also spilling into diplomacy, with France summoning Iran's ambassador over what it calls a disinformation campaign about the protests.

topStories.headline: Missile Fired at International Airport Just Before Passengers Landed Amid Iran War
topStories.whyItMatters: The near-miss at a civilian airport shows the seven-month war is edging closer to everyday travelers and commercial aviation. US officials are demanding Iran make a 'meaningful' cut to its nuclear program to end the conflict, and Putin has now offered to mediate.

topStories.headline: Pakistan Confirms Troop Deployment to Saudi Arabia Under New Defense Pact
topStories.whyItMatters: The 'Mecca pact' is bringing Pakistani and Turkish forces in to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks, widening the roster of countries involved in the Middle East conflict. More foreign troops in the region raises the stakes and could keep oil prices, and your gas bill, elevated.

topStories.headline: US Mortgage Rates Hit Three-Year High
topStories.whyItMatters: Borrowing costs for homebuyers are now the steepest since early in the decade, and applications have dropped to their lowest level since February. If you're planning to buy a home, refinance, or finance a car, expect to pay noticeably more than you would have even a year ago.

topStories.headline: Trump Floats Suspending the Federal Gas Tax as War Strains the Economy
topStories.whyItMatters: With oil prices carrying a war premium and drivers paying more at the pump, the White House is considering a temporary break on the federal gas tax. Any relief would be modest, and critics note it would reduce funding for road and infrastructure repairs.

topStories.headline: Kyiv Faces Water and Power Cuts as Emergency Blackouts Spread Across Ukraine
topStories.whyItMatters: Sustained strikes on infrastructure mean ordinary Ukrainians are facing scheduled blackouts and disrupted water supplies heading into colder months. The grinding toll on civilians keeps pressure on Western governments for more air defense support.

topStories.headline: WHO Says It Can't Fully Assess Russia's Plague Situation as Second Case Emerges
topStories.whyItMatters: Health officials want more transparency after reports of a second plague case in Russia, which Moscow insists poses no risk to the population. Limited information from health authorities makes it harder to judge whether there's any broader public health concern.

whatWeAreWatching: Whether Iran agrees to a 'meaningful' reduction of its nuclear program, the stated US condition for ending the seven-month war, and whether Putin's offer to mediate gains traction.
Whether France's suspension of stun grenades and promised concessions calm the student protests or if more of the country's schools join the walkouts this week.
The pace of Pakistani and Turkish military deployments to Saudi Arabia, and whether the Houthis respond with new attacks on shipping or Saudi territory.
Whether the proposed federal gas tax suspension moves forward in Washington and how much actual relief shows up at the pump.
Where mortgage rates head next week after hitting a three-year high, a key signal for anyone weighing a home purchase or refinance.
Whether Russia grants health inspectors fuller access to investigate the reported plague cases.
